stem: A 70-year-old woman had a femoral neck fracture repaired two days ago. Before the fall she lived alone, shopped and climbed stairs without help. She is alert and oriented, and examination is unremarkable. The team plans her rehabilitation and wants to estimate how well she will recover.
oneliner: 70F + operative femoral fracture repair 2 days ago + independent before the fall + alert → which factor best predicts rehabilitation success?
ask: Which factor best predicts her rehabilitation outcome?

options.A: Her level of function before the fracture
options.B: Her age of 70 years at the time of injury
options.C: Her postoperative hemoglobin on the second day
options.D: Her serum calcium at admission to hospital
options.E: Her serum vitamin D level before surgery

whyNot.B: Age matters, but **baseline function** predicts recovery more strongly
whyNot.C: A single postoperative value reflects **surgical blood loss**, not her **ability to walk again**
whyNot.D: An admission value says nothing about her **pre-fall mobility**, which drives recovery
whyNot.E: Matters for **bone health**, but it does not predict how well she will **regain function**

answer: Her pre-fracture level of activity and function
why: The **best predictor of recovery** after hip fracture is **pre-fracture function and activity**: those who walked and lived independently before are likely to do so again. **Cognition** also matters, and she is oriented.
chain: Frail or dependent patients often do not

idea.rule: After a hip fracture, the patient returns toward where they started.
also: Dementia and delirium predict poor recovery
Early surgery within 48 hours lowers mortality
Many patients do not regain pre-fracture mobility
Prevent with bone-protective drugs and fall reduction

stem: A 22-year-old man fell on his outstretched right hand during a basketball game. The wrist is tender in the anatomic snuffbox, and a CT scan shows an undisplaced fracture through the waist of the scaphoid. It is treated with a cast. He asks what problem might arise at the fracture site.
oneliner: 22M + fall on outstretched hand + snuffbox tenderness + scaphoid waist fracture → which complication is he most at risk of?

options.A: Median nerve injury from volar displacement
options.B: Thrombosis of the radial artery at the wrist
options.D: Complex regional pain syndrome of the hand
options.E: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole

whyNot.A: Seen with **lunate dislocation**; he has an **undisplaced scaphoid** fracture
whyNot.B: Possible after wrist trauma, but far less likely than **nonunion or necrosis**
whyNot.C: Complicates **forearm fractures or crush**, with severe pain on passive stretch
whyNot.D: Can follow any fracture, but the **scaphoid's own blood supply** is the greater risk

answer: Avascular necrosis and nonunion of the proximal scaphoid
why: The scaphoid's blood supply enters **distally** and runs retrograde, so a fracture through the waist can cut off the **proximal pole**. That leads to **avascular necrosis and nonunion**, and later wrist arthritis.

idea.rule: Retrograde blood supply makes the proximal pole the part that dies.
also: Scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone
Femoral head and talus also have retrograde supply

stem: A 31-year-old man falls from a ladder onto an outstretched hand. The wrist has marked central swelling on the palm side just proximal to the crease, and the anatomic snuffbox is not tender. A lateral x-ray shows the lunate tilted and displaced out of its normal cup while the other carpal bones stay aligned with the radius.
oneliner: 31M + ladder fall on outstretched hand + central volar wrist swelling + snuffbox not tender + lunate tilted out of its cup → which complication is he at risk of?

options.A: Ulnar nerve compression in Guyon canal
options.C: Radial nerve injury at the wrist
options.D: Avascular necrosis of the scaphoid proximal pole
options.E: Anterior interosseous nerve injury at the forearm

whyNot.A: Guyon canal lies on the **ulnar side**; his swelling is **central**, over the carpal tunnel
whyNot.C: The radial sensory branch runs **dorsally**; his mass is on the **palm side**
whyNot.D: Follows **scaphoid fracture** with snuffbox tenderness, which is absent
whyNot.E: This nerve branches **in the forearm**, above the displaced lunate at the **wrist**

answer: Acute carpal tunnel syndrome from median nerve compression
why: A **volarly displaced lunate** pushes into the carpal tunnel and **compresses the median nerve**, causing **acute carpal tunnel syndrome** with numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers. It needs urgent reduction. The negative snuffbox argues against a scaphoid injury.
chain: Numbness of thumb, index, middle fingers; weak thenar muscles

idea.rule: A displaced carpal bone in the tunnel squeezes the median nerve first.
also: Perilunate injury has the capitate dislocated dorsally
Lunate dislocation can look like a spilled teacup on lateral x-ray
Thenar muscle weakness appears in late median compression
